Test each proposed set of exponents against the quantity named.
**Step 1 — angular frequency.** ω = 2πf, measured in **rad s⁻¹**:
[ω] = **M⁰ L⁰ T⁻¹** ✓
which is exactly a = 0, b = 0, c = −1 ✓ **correct**
**Step 2 — force.** F = ma:
[F] = **M¹ L¹ T⁻²** ✓ but the option states c = **+2** ✗ the sign is wrong.
**Step 3 — spring constant.** k = F/x:
[k] = [M L T⁻²]/[L] = **M¹ L⁰ T⁻²** ✓ but the option states b = **−1** ✗
**Step 4 — surface tension.** S = force per unit length:
[S] = [M L T⁻²]/[L] = **M¹ L⁰ T⁻²** ✓ but the option states b = **+1** ✗
**Step 5 — conclude.** Only the **angular frequency** entry is right ✓
**Why ω has no mass or length.** It is a **rate of rotation** - an angle per unit
time ✓ and the radian is **dimensionless**, being a ratio of two lengths. So only the
reciprocal of time survives.
**The curiosity about k and S.** The spring constant and surface tension have the
**same** dimensions, M T⁻² ✓ one being force per length and the other force per unit
length of boundary. Their units - N m⁻¹ - are identical, though the quantities are
quite different physically.
**Why both options get them wrong.** Each attaches a non-zero power of L ✓ but
dividing a force by a length removes the length entirely.
**The force entry's error.** T⁻² is required, not T⁺² ✓ A positive power of time would
make the force **grow** with the square of the time scale, which is meaningless.
**Why dimensional analysis is worth doing.** It catches errors instantly ✓ and it can
even suggest the form of an unknown relation - as in the sixth-power law for the mass
of a stone moved by a river.
**Its limitation.** It cannot find **dimensionless** constants ✓ The period of a
pendulum comes out as √(l/g) by dimensions, but the 2π must come from the full
analysis.
**Other quantities with ω's dimensions.** Frequency, angular velocity, decay constant
and velocity gradient - all **T⁻¹** ✓ Dimensional identity never implies physical
identity.
**Reading the distractors.** Each misstates one exponent ✓ Working out the dimensions
of all four quantities and comparing takes only a moment.
∴ angular frequency if a = 0, b = 0, c = −1.

For a product of powers, each relative error is multiplied by the **magnitude** of its
exponent, and all of them **add**.
**Step 1 — state the rule.** For Q = x³y²/z,
ΔQ/Q = **3(Δx/x) + 2(Δy/y) + 1(Δz/z)** ✓
**Step 2 — substitute the percentages.**
from x: 3 x 1% = **3%**
from y: 2 x 2% = **4%**
from z: 1 x 4% = **4%** ✓
**Step 3 — add.**
3 + 4 + 4 = **11%** ✓
**Why the z error is not subtracted.** Errors never cancel ✓ A quantity in the
**denominator** contributes just as much uncertainty as one in the numerator, so the
**magnitude** of its exponent is used and the contributions are summed. Subtracting
would assume a cancellation we have no right to expect.
**Why the exponents multiply the errors.** Taking logarithms and differentiating:
ln Q = 3 ln x + 2 ln y − ln z ✓
ΔQ/Q = 3Δx/x + 2Δy/y − Δz/z, and the magnitudes are taken for the worst case ✓
**Which measurement matters most.** The **x** cubed and the **z** each contribute 3-4
percentage points ✓ x is the most precisely measured but its error is tripled; z is
the least precise but enters only once. Both deserve attention equally.
**The practical lesson.** Improving a measurement helps only if its **weighted**
contribution is large ✓ Halving the error in y would save only 2 percentage points out
of 11.
**A worked check.** Suppose x, y and z are each 100, so Q = 10⁶ x 10⁴/100 = 10⁸. With
x 1% high, y 2% high and z 4% low:
Q′ = (101)³(102)²/96 = 1·030 x 1·040/0·96 x 10⁸ = **1·116 x 10⁸** ✓ an increase of
**11·6%**, close to the 11% the linear rule predicts.
**Why the rule is only approximate.** It drops second-order terms ✓ Good for errors of
a few per cent, as here; for large errors the exact calculation is needed.
**The statistical alternative.** In quadrature,
√(3² + 4² + 4²) = **6·4%** ✓ less pessimistic, and appropriate when the errors are
**independent and random**. The school convention uses the simple sum, giving the
maximum possible error.
**Reading the distractors.** **4%**, **3%** and **1%** ✗ each count only one of the
three contributions ✓
∴ 11 %.

Planck's constant divided by moment of inertia has the dimensions of **frequency**.
**Step 1 — write the dimensions of h.** From E = hν:
[h] = [M L² T⁻²]/[T⁻¹] = **[M L² T⁻¹]** ✓
**Step 2 — write the dimensions of I.** From I = mr²:
[I] = **[M L²]** ✓
**Step 3 — divide.**
[h/I] = [M L² T⁻¹]/[M L²]
= **[T⁻¹]** ✓
**Step 4 — name it.** T⁻¹ is a **frequency** ✓
**Why this combination is physically meaningful.** h/I is, to within factors of 2π,
the **rotational energy spacing** of a molecule divided by h ✓ The rotational levels
of a rigid rotor are
E_J = J(J + 1)ℏ²/2I ✓
so the transition frequencies are multiples of **ℏ/I** - which is why microwave
rotational spectra give molecular moments of inertia, and hence bond lengths, with
great precision.
**A worked instance.** For carbon monoxide, I = **1·45 x 10⁻⁴⁶ kg m²**:
ℏ/I = 1·055 x 10⁻³⁴/1·45 x 10⁻⁴⁶ = **7·3 x 10¹¹ Hz** ✓ in the microwave region, which
is exactly where CO's rotational spectrum is found.
**Why h shares its dimensions with angular momentum.** [M L² T⁻¹] is exactly mvr ✓
which is why ℏ is the natural **quantum of angular momentum**, and why L = nℏ in the
Bohr model.
**The quickest route to the answer.** Recognise h as an **angular momentum** and I as
a **moment of inertia** ✓ Their ratio is L/I = **ω**, an angular velocity - and angular
velocity has the dimensions of frequency.
**Why frequency and angular momentum are not the same thing.** Dimensional identity
never implies physical identity ✓ as work and torque famously show. Here, though, the
ratio really is an angular frequency.
**Other quantities with T⁻¹.** Angular velocity, decay constant, velocity gradient,
Rydberg constant times c ✓
**Why the radian is dimensionless.** It is a ratio of arc to radius ✓ so rad s⁻¹ and
s⁻¹ have the same dimensions, though they are distinguished in practice.
**Reading the distractors.** **Time** ✗ is the reciprocal, I/h. **Angular momentum** ✗
is h itself, and **velocity** ✗ would need L T⁻¹ ✓ Working out each dimension
separately settles it.
∴ frequency.

Antiparallel currents **repel**, with force per unit length **2 x 10⁻⁷ I₁I₂/d**.
**Step 1 — write the formula.**
F/L = µ₀I₁I₂/(2πd)
= **2 x 10⁻⁷ I₁I₂/d** ✓
**Step 2 — substitute.**
F/L = 2 x 10⁻⁷ x (1)(3)/1
= **6 x 10⁻⁷ N m⁻¹** ✓
**Step 3 — find the direction.** The currents are in **opposite** directions, so the
force is **repulsive** ✓
**The rule for parallel conductors.**
**same** direction → **attract** ✓
**opposite** directions → **repel** ✓
**Why opposite currents repel.** Each wire sits in the other's magnetic field, and
F̄ = I L̄ x B̄ works out **outward** when the currents oppose ✓ The two halves of a
hairpin conductor fly apart for this reason, and a coil carrying a large pulse tries to
unwind itself.
**Why the constant is 2 x 10⁻⁷.**
µ₀/2π = (4π x 10⁻⁷)/2π = **2 x 10⁻⁷** exactly ✓ a convenient number that arises
because µ₀ was **defined** as 4π x 10⁻⁷ until 2019.
**The historical definition of the ampere.** One ampere is the current which, in two
infinite parallel wires **one metre apart** in vacuum, produces a force of
**2 x 10⁻⁷ N per metre** ✓ Setting I₁ = I₂ = 1 and d = 1 in the formula reproduces
exactly that - which is why the constant looks so contrived.
**Why the ampere was redefined in 2019.** It is now fixed by assigning an exact value
to the **elementary charge** e ✓ so µ₀ is no longer exact but must be measured - though
its value is unchanged to ten significant figures.
**How small the force is.** 6 x 10⁻⁷ N per metre is about the weight of a **60
microgram** speck ✓ which is why the definition required such painstaking
experiments with current balances.
**Where the force becomes significant.** In **busbars** carrying thousands of amperes,
and in the windings of large electromagnets ✓ A short-circuit current of 100 kA in
bars 10 cm apart gives 20 kN per metre - enough to tear the installation apart, which
is why busbars are heavily braced.
**The field one wire produces at the other.**
B = 2 x 10⁻⁷(1)/1 = **2 x 10⁻⁷ T** ✓ and F/L = BI₂ = 2 x 10⁻⁷ x 3 = 6 x 10⁻⁷ ✓
confirming the answer by a second route.
**Reading the distractors.** **6 x 10⁻⁷ attractive** ✗ has the magnitude right but the
direction wrong. The **10⁻⁵** options ✗ are a hundred times too large ✓
∴ 6 × 10⁻⁷ Nm⁻¹ repulsive.

At the zero-order maximum **all** wavelengths arrive in phase, so the central fringe is
**white**.
**Step 1 — write the grating condition.**
d sin θ = **nλ** ✓
**Step 2 — set n = 0.**
d sin θ = 0, so **θ = 0** ✓ for **every** wavelength.
**Step 3 — see the consequence.** All the colours of the incident light are brought to
the **same** point, straight ahead ✓ Recombining, they give **white**.
**Why the higher orders are coloured.** For n ≥ 1,
sin θ = **nλ/d** ✓ which depends on λ ✓ Violet, with the shortest wavelength, is
deviated **least** and red most - so each order spreads into a spectrum.
**The contrast with a prism.** A prism deviates **violet** most; a grating deviates
**red** most ✓ The two spectra are reversed, which is a quick way of telling how a
spectrum was produced.
**Why the central maximum is the brightest.** No light is dispersed away from it ✓ The
intensity falls off rapidly with order, which is why high-order spectra are faint.
**Why the orders overlap at high n.** The second-order red at 700 nm sits at the same
angle as the third-order at 467 nm ✓ so beyond the second order the spectra run into
one another - a practical limit on the useful orders.
**What a grating is.** Thousands of parallel slits or grooves per centimetre ✓ with d
the spacing. A typical grating has 600 lines per mm, giving d = **1·67 µm**.
**Why a grating beats a prism for spectroscopy.** Its dispersion is **greater** and,
more importantly, **calculable** from d and n alone ✓ whereas a prism's depends on the
glass's dispersion curve. Gratings also work far into the infrared and ultraviolet.
**The resolving power.**
R = λ/Δλ = **nN** ✓ with N the number of illuminated lines. A grating with 10000 lines
resolves 0·06 nm in the first order - enough to split the sodium D lines.
**Why the zero order is wasted light.** It carries no spectral information ✓ which is
why **blazed** gratings are shaped to throw most of the light into a chosen higher
order instead.
**Reading the distractors.** "**Spectrum of the colours**" ✗ describes the first and
higher orders. "**Absent**" ✗ - it is the brightest of all. "**One of the component
colours**" ✗ would need the condition to single out a wavelength, which n = 0 does
not ✓
∴ white.

H-polaroid is made by **stretching polyvinyl alcohol** and **impregnating it with
iodine**.
**Step 1 — stretch the film.** Sheets of **polyvinyl alcohol** are heated and
stretched, which aligns the long polymer chains **parallel** to one another ✓
**Step 2 — impregnate with iodine.** The sheet is dipped in an iodine solution ✓ The
iodine attaches along the aligned chains, forming long conducting chains of its own.
**Step 3 — see how it polarises.** Electrons move freely **along** the iodine chains,
absorbing the component of the light's electric field parallel to them ✓ The
perpendicular component passes through. The sheet is therefore **dichroic**, and the
transmitted light is plane-polarised.
**Why the pass axis is perpendicular to the stretch.** The absorbed component is the
one **along** the chains ✓ so what survives vibrates **across** them - a point that
often surprises.
**The inventor.** **Edwin Land**, 1929, while still a student ✓ He founded the Polaroid
Corporation on it, and the sheet polariser transformed optics from a laboratory
curiosity into an everyday material.
**The earlier type.** **K-polaroid** used stretched polyvinyl alcohol **dehydrated**
with a catalyst, forming polyvinylene ✓ which is the first option - a real material,
but not H-polaroid.
**The still earlier type.** **J-polaroid** used aligned crystals of **herapathite** -
quinine iodosulphate - embedded in nitrocellulose ✓ the third option, Land's own first
attempt, soon superseded.
**Why synthetic polarisers displaced tourmaline.** A natural dichroic crystal is small,
expensive and strongly coloured ✓ Polaroid sheet can be made in square metres, cheaply,
and is nearly neutral in colour.
**Where polaroids are used.** Sunglasses, camera filters, LCD screens, stress analysis,
3-D cinema glasses and microscopy ✓ Every liquid-crystal display has two of them, with
the liquid crystal rotating the polarisation between.
**Malus's law, which governs two in series.**
I = I₀cos²θ ✓ full transmission when parallel, extinction when crossed.
**What polarisation proves.** That light is a **transverse** wave ✓ A longitudinal wave
has no plane of vibration to select, so sound cannot be polarised.
**Reading the distractors.** The **dehydrating agent** ✗ makes K-polaroid; the
**herapathite** ✗ makes J-polaroid; **tourmaline** ✗ is the natural crystal ✓ Only
iodine gives the H type.
∴ stretching polyvinyl alcohol and then impregnating with iodine.

The central bright fringe spans **2λD/a**.
**Step 1 — locate the first minimum.** For a single slit,
a sin θ = λ ✓
so for small angles θ = **λ/a** on each side.
**Step 2 — convert to a distance on the screen.**
y = Dθ = **λD/a** ✓ from the centre to the first dark fringe.
**Step 3 — double it.** The question asks for the distance **between** the first dark
fringes on either side:
width = **2λD/a** ✓
**Step 4 — substitute.**
= 2(600 x 10⁻⁹)(2)/(1 x 10⁻³)
= 2·4 x 10⁻⁶/10⁻³ ✓
**Step 5 — evaluate.**
= 2·4 x 10⁻³ m
= **2·4 mm** ✓
**Why the central maximum is twice as wide as the others.** It runs from the first
minimum on one side to the first on the other ✓ while each secondary maximum occupies
only the interval between consecutive minima, λD/a.
**How the intensity is distributed.** About **84%** of the light falls in the central
band ✓ the first secondary maximum carrying only 4·7% - which is why a single slit
shows one bright band with faint wings.
**Why a narrower slit spreads the light more.** y ∝ **1/a** ✓ Narrowing the slit widens
the pattern - the counter-intuitive hallmark of diffraction, and a direct expression of
the uncertainty principle applied to the photon's transverse momentum.
**Why "from a distant source" matters.** It guarantees **plane** wavefronts at the
slit ✓ the Fraunhofer condition, under which the simple formula holds. A nearby source
would need the fuller Fresnel treatment.
**The angular width.**
2θ = 2λ/a = 2(600 x 10⁻⁹)/10⁻³ = **1·2 x 10⁻³ rad** ✓ about 0·07° - small, which is why
diffraction goes unnoticed with everyday apertures.
**When ray optics suffices.** When the slit is much wider than the wavelength ✓ Here
a/λ = 1667, so the spreading is slight but measurable. Shrink the slit to 10 µm and the
pattern spreads over 7°.
**The contrast with the double slit.** There the fringes are **equally** spaced at
λD/d ✓ and the single-slit pattern forms an **envelope** modulating their brightness.
**Reading the distractors.** **1·2 mm** ✗ is the half-width, centre to first minimum -
the commonest slip. **1·2 cm** and **2·4 cm** ✗ are ten times too large ✓
∴ 2.4 mm.

The wave theory of light was first put forward by **Christiaan Huygens**.
**Step 1 — recall the date and the work.** Huygens proposed it in **1678** and
published it in his *Traite de la Lumiere* in 1690 ✓ Light, he argued, is a
**longitudinal** disturbance in an all-pervading **aether**.
**Step 2 — recall his central idea.** **Huygens' principle**: every point on a
wavefront acts as a source of secondary **wavelets**, and the new wavefront is their
common **tangent** ✓
**What it explained.** **Reflection**, **refraction** and the **double refraction** of
calcite - the last being quite beyond the particle theory ✓ It also predicted, rightly,
that light travels **slower** in a denser medium.
**Why it was neglected for a century.** **Newton's** rival **corpuscular** theory
carried his immense authority ✓ and Huygens' theory could not then account for
**rectilinear propagation** - why light casts sharp shadows rather than bending round
corners.
**Who revived it.** **Thomas Young**, with the **double-slit** experiment of 1801 ✓
Interference is inexplicable on a particle theory, and his work made the wave picture
unavoidable.
**Who completed it.** **Augustin Fresnel**, in the 1810s ✓ He combined Huygens'
construction with Young's interference to explain **diffraction** mathematically, and
showed that the sharp shadows follow from the **shortness** of the wavelength.
**The decisive experiment.** **Foucault**, 1850, measured the speed of light in water
and found it **slower** than in air ✓ exactly as the wave theory required and contrary
to Newton's prediction.
**Where Huygens was wrong.** He thought light **longitudinal** ✓ Polarisation, studied
by Young and Fresnel, showed it to be **transverse** - and Maxwell later identified
the oscillating quantities as electric and magnetic fields.
**The modern view.** Light is **both** wave and particle ✓ The wave picture explains
interference and diffraction; the photon picture the photoelectric and Compton
effects. Huygens had half the truth, and Newton the other half.
**Why Huygens' principle is still taught.** It remains the simplest route to the laws
of reflection and refraction, and to the whole of diffraction theory ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **Newton** ✗ championed the **corpuscular** theory.
**Young** ✗ and **Fresnel** ✗ revived and developed the wave theory, but did not
originate it ✓
∴ Christian Huygens.

The diffraction width goes as **λ/a**, so a longer wavelength and a narrower slit both
widen it.
**Step 1 — write the width.** For a single slit,
width ∝ **λ/a** ✓
**Step 2 — apply the two changes.**
wavelength: 400 nm → 600 nm, a factor of **1·5** ✓
slit width: a → a/2, a factor of **2** ✓
**Step 3 — combine.**
new width = y x 1·5 x 2
= **3y** ✓
**Why both changes widen the pattern.** A longer wavelength diffracts more, and a
narrower slit diffracts more ✓ The two effects **multiply**, and the pattern triples.
**Why a narrower slit spreads the light.** θ = λ/a ✓ Squeezing the beam in space
spreads it in **angle** - the optical statement of the **uncertainty principle**:
confining the transverse position increases the spread of transverse momentum.
**A worked check.** With D = 1 m:
originally: 2λD/a = 2(400 x 10⁻⁹)/a
after: 2(600 x 10⁻⁹)/(a/2) = 2400 x 10⁻⁹/a ✓
and 2400/800 = **3** ✓ exactly three times.
**Why the pattern does not vanish.** Covering half the slit reduces the **light**, but
the surviving half still diffracts - more strongly, in fact ✓ The first option, that
the pattern disappears, mistakes blocking part of a slit for blocking it entirely.
**What does change besides the width.** The **intensity** falls, since less light
enters ✓ and the colour changes from violet to yellow. The **shape** of the pattern -
a broad central band with faint wings - is unaltered.
**The limiting case.** If a became comparable with λ, the pattern would spread over
**all** angles and the slit would radiate almost like a point source ✓ Here
a/λ remains large, so the pattern is still a recognisable band.
**Why the central maximum is the one measured.** It is much the brightest and its edges
- the first minima - are sharply defined ✓ which makes its width the standard measure
of a diffraction pattern.
**The underlying formula.**
y = **2λD/a** ✓ linear in λ, inverse in a, and proportional to the screen distance.
**Reading the distractors.** The option that the pattern **vanishes** ✗ misreads
"half the slit covered". Options giving a **smaller** width ✗ reverse both
dependences ✓
∴ 3y.
